1: [![Nuget](https://img.shields.io/nuget/v/Generator.Equals)](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Generator.Equals/)
2: # Generator.Equals
3: 
4: A C# source generator that automatically implements `IEquatable<T>`, `Equals`, and `GetHashCode` — using just attributes.
5: 
6: Writing correct equality logic in C# is tedious, error-prone, and easy to forget when adding new properties. Generator.Equals eliminates that boilerplate by generating efficient, best-practice equality code at compile time.
7: 
8: ### Why use Generator.Equals?
9: 
10: - **Zero boilerplate** — Mark your type with `[Equatable]` and the generator does the rest. No hand-written `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, or `==`/`!=` operators.
11: - **Collection-aware** — Compare arrays, lists, dictionaries, and sets by value out of the box with `[OrderedEquality]`, `[UnorderedEquality]`, and `[SetEquality]`.
12: - **Highly customizable** — Use `[CustomEquality]`, `[StringEquality]`, `[PrecisionEquality]`, `[ReferenceEquality]`, or `[IgnoreEquality]` to control comparison per-property.
13: - **Works everywhere** — Supports classes, structs, records, and record structs.
14: - **Inheritance-friendly** — Correctly chains `base.Equals()` across deep inheritance hierarchies and inherits equality attributes from overridden properties.
15: - **Structured diffs** — Call `Inequalities()` to get exactly which members differ between two instances, with full paths into nested objects, collections, and dictionaries.
16: - **Compile-time only** — No reflection or IL injection. The generator emits plain C# source code that you can inspect and debug.
17: 
18: ----------------
19: ## Requirements
20: 
21: In order to use this library, you must:
22: * Use a target framework that supports .NET Standard >= 2.0
23: * Set your project's C# ```LangVersion``` property to 9.0 or higher.
24: 
25: ## Installation
26: 
27: Simply add the package `Generator.Equals` to your project. Keep reading to learn how to add the attributes to your types.
28: 
29: ## Usage
30: 
31: The below sample shows how to use Generator.Equals to override the default equality implementation for a C# record, enhancing it with the ability to determine the equality between the array contents of the record.
32: 
33: ```c#
34: using Generator.Equals;
35: 
36: [Equatable]
37: partial record MyRecord(
38:     [property: OrderedEquality] string[] Fruits
39: );
40: 
41: class Program
42: {
43:     static void Main(string[] args)
44:     {
45:         var record1 = new MyRecord(new[] {"banana", "apple"});
46:         var record2 = new MyRecord(new[] {"banana", "apple"});
47:         var record3 = new MyRecord(new[] {"banana", "cherry"});
48: 
49:         // Use the generated == operator
50:         Console.WriteLine(record1 == record2); // True
51: 
52:         // Use the generated comparer directly
53:         Console.WriteLine(MyRecord.EqualityComparer.Default.Equals(record1, record3)); // False
54: 
55:         // List exactly which members differ between two instances
56:         foreach (var diff in MyRecord.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(record1, record3))
57:             Console.WriteLine(diff);
58:         // Output:
59:         //   Fruits[1]: apple → cherry
60:     }
61: }
62: ```
63: Need more than records? Generator.Equals supports properties (and fields) also across classes, structs and record structs.
64: 
65: ```c#
66: using Generator.Equals;
67: 
68: [Equatable]
69: partial class MyClass
70: {
71:     [DefaultEquality] 
72:     private int _secretNumber = 42;
73: 
74:     [OrderedEquality] 
75:     public string[] Fruits { get; set; }
76: }
77: 
78: [Equatable]
79: partial struct MyStruct
80: {
81:     [OrderedEquality] 
82:     public string[] Fruits { get; set; }
83: }
84: 
85: [Equatable]
86: partial record struct MyRecordStruct(
87:     [property: OrderedEquality] string[] Fruits
88: );
89: ```
90: 
91: ## Supported Comparers
92: 
93: Below is a list of all supported comparers. Would you like something else added? Let me know by raising an issue or sending a PR!
94: 
95: ### Default
96: 
97: This is the comparer that's used when a property has no attributes indicating otherwise. The generated code will use 
98: ```EqualityComparer<T>.Default``` for both equals and hashing operation.
99: 
100: > _Fields are not used in comparison unless explicitly annotated. To enable the default comparison for a field, annotate it with the `DefaultEquality` attribute._
101: 
102: ### IgnoreEquality
103: 
104: ```c#
105: [IgnoreEquality] 
106: public string Name { get; set; }
107: ```
108: 
109: As the name implies, the property is ignored during Equals and GetHashCode calls!
110: 
111: 
112: ### OrderedEquality
113: 
114: ```c#
115: [OrderedEquality]
116: public string[] Fruits { get; set; } // Fruits have to be in the same order for the array to be considered equal.
117: ```
118: 
119: This equality comparer will compare properties as a sequence instead of a reference. This works just like ```Enumerable.SequenceEqual```, which assumes both lists are of the same size and same sort.
120: 
121: Bear in mind that the property has to implement IEnumerable<T> and the that the items themselves implement equality (you can use Generator.Equals in the items too!).
122: 
123: You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:
124: 
125: ```c#
126: // Using StringComparison for string collections
127: [OrderedEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
128: public string[] Tags { get; set; }
129: 
130: // Using a custom comparer type
131: [OrderedEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
132: public string[] Names { get; set; }
133: 
134: // Using a custom IEqualityComparer<T> with a Default static member
135: [OrderedEquality(typeof(MyCustomComparer))]
136: public string[] Values { get; set; }
137: ```
138: 
139: ### UnorderedEquality
140: 
141: ```c#
142: [UnorderedEquality]
143: public string[] Fruits { get; set; } // Does not care about the order of the fruits!
144: 
145: [UnorderedEquality]
146: public IDictionary<string, object> Properties { get; set; } // Works with dictionaries too!
147: ```
148: 
149: This equality comparer will compare properties as an unordered sequence instead of a reference. This works just like ```Enumerable.SequenceEqual```, but it does not care about the order as long as the all values (including the repetitions) are present.
150: 
151: As with OrderedEquality, bear in mind that the property (or key and values if using a dictionary) has to implement IEnumerable<T> and the that the items themselves implement equality (you can use Generator.Equals in the items too!).
152: 
153: You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:
154: 
155: ```c#
156: // Using StringComparison for string collections
157: [UnorderedEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
158: public List<string> Tags { get; set; }
159: 
160: // Using a custom comparer type
161: [UnorderedEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
162: public List<string> Names { get; set; }
163: ```
164: 
165: ### SetEquality
166: 
167: ```c#
168: [SetEquality]
169: public HashSet<string> Fruits { get; set; } // Fruits can be in any order and duplicates are ignored
170: ```
171: 
172: This equality comparer will do a set comparison, using ```SetEquals``` whenever the underlying collection implements `ISet<T>`, otherwise falling back to manually comparing both collections, which can be expensive for large collections.
173: 
174: You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:
175: 
176: ```c#
177: // Using StringComparison for string collections
178: [SetEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
179: public HashSet<string> Tags { get; set; }
180: 
181: // Using a custom comparer type
182: [SetEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
183: public HashSet<string> Names { get; set; }
184: ```
185: 
186: Hashing always returns 0 for this type of equality.
187: 
188: ### ReferenceEquality
189: 
190: ```c#
191: [ReferenceEquality] 
192: public string Name { get; set; } // Will only return true if strings are the same reference (eg. when used with string.Intern)
193: ```
194: 
195: This will ignore whatever equality is implemented for a particular object and compare references instead.
196: 
197: ### StringEquality
198: 
199: ```c#
200: [StringEquality(StringComparison.CurrentCulture | CurrentCultureIgnoreCase | InvariantCulture | InvariantCultureIgnoreCase | Ordinal | OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
201: public string Title { get; set; } // Will use the StringComparison set in constructor when comparing strings
202: ```
203: 
204: ### PrecisionEquality
205: 
206: ```c#
207: [PrecisionEquality(0.001)]
208: public double Temperature { get; set; } // Equal if Math.Abs(a - b) < 0.001
209: 
210: [PrecisionEquality(5)]
211: public int Score { get; set; } // Equal if Math.Abs(a - b) < 5
212: 
213: [PrecisionEquality(0.001)]
214: public double? NullableValue { get; set; } // Handles nulls: both null = equal, one null = not equal
215: ```
216: 
217: This equality comparer uses a tolerance (epsilon) to compare numeric values. Two values are considered equal when their absolute difference is less than the specified precision. This is excluded from `GetHashCode` since there is no stable bucketing under tolerance.
218: 
219: Supported types: `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `int`, `long`, `short`, `sbyte`, and their nullable variants.
220: 
221: ### CustomEquality
222: 
223: ```c#
224: class LengthEqualityComparer : IEqualityComparer<string>
225: {
226:     public static readonly LengthEqualityComparer Default = new();
227: 
228:     public bool Equals(string? x, string? y) => x?.Length == y?.Length;
229: 
230:     public int GetHashCode(string obj) => obj.Length.GetHashCode();
231: }
232: 
233: class NameEqualityComparer 
234: {
235:     public static readonly IEqualityComparer<string> Default = new SomeCustomComparer();
236: }
237: 
238: 
239: [CustomEquality(typeof(LengthEqualityComparer))] 
240: public string Name1 { get; set; } // Will use LengthEqualityComparer to compare the values of Name1.
241: 
242: [CustomEquality(typeof(NameEqualityComparer))] 
243: public string Name2 { get; set; } // Will use NameEqualityComparer.Default to compare values of Name2.
244: 
245: [CustomEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))] 
246: public string Name2 { get; set; } // Will use StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase to compare values of Name2.
247: ```
248: 
249: This attribute allows you to specify a custom comparer for a particular property. For it to work, the type passed as an
250: argument to CustomEqualityAttribute should fulfill AT LEAST one of the following:
251: 
252: * Have a static field/property named Default returning a valid IEqualityComparer<T> instance for the target type;
253: * Have a static field/property with the same name passed to the CustomComparerAttribute returning a valid IEqualityComparer<T> instance for the target type;
254: * Implement IEqualityComparer<T> and expose a parameterless constructor.
255: 
256: ## Advanced Options
257: 
258: ### Explicit Mode
259: 
260: The generator allows you to explicitly specify which properties are used to generate the `IEquatable`.  
261: 
262: To do this, set the `Explicit` property of `EquatableAttribute` to `true` and specify the required properties using `DefaultEqualityAttribute` or other attributes.
263: ```cs
264: using Generator.Equals;
265: 
266: [Equatable(Explicit = true)]
267: partial class MyClass
268: {
269:     // Only this property will be used for equality!
270:     [DefaultEquality] 
271:     public string Name { get; set; } = "Konstantin"; 
272:     
273:     public string Description { get; set; } = "";
274: }
275: ```
276: 
277: 
278: ### Ignore Inherited Members
279: 
280: By default (`IgnoreInheritedMembers = false`), the generated code handles inherited members as follows:
281: - If any ancestor has `[Equatable]` or a custom `Equals` override, `base.Equals()` is called to delegate equality
282: - If NO ancestor has `[Equatable]`, all inherited properties from the entire chain are explicitly compared
283: 
284: Set `IgnoreInheritedMembers = true` to skip calling `base.Equals()` and ignore all inherited properties.
285: This is useful when you want to completely redefine equality for a derived class without considering
286: the base class's properties.
287: 
288: ```cs
289: using Generator.Equals;
290: 
291: [Equatable]
292: partial class Person
293: {
294:     public string Name { get; set; }
295: }
296: 
297: [Equatable(IgnoreInheritedMembers = true)]
298: partial class Doctor : Person
299: {
300:     // Will NOT call base.Equals(), so Person.Name is not compared.
301:     // Only Id and Specialization are used for equality.
302:     public string Id { get; set; }
303:     public string Specialization { get; set; }
304: }
305: ```
306: 
307: ## Inequalities
308: 
309: Every `[Equatable]` type gets a generated `EqualityComparer` with an `Inequalities()` method that returns exactly which members differ between two instances — with full member paths, including nested objects, collection indices, and dictionary keys.
310: 
311: ```c#
312: [Equatable]
313: partial record Customer
314: {
315:     public required string Name { get; init; }
316:     [UnorderedEquality] public required ImmutableDictionary<string, Address> Addresses { get; init; }
317: }
318: 
319: [Equatable]
320: partial record Address
321: {
322:     public required string Street { get; init; }
323:     public required string City { get; init; }
324: }
325: ```
326: 
327: ```c#
328: var original = new Customer
329: {
330:     Name = "John Doe",
331:     Addresses = ImmutableDictionary<string, Address>.Empty
332:         .Add("home", new Address { Street = "123 Main St", City = "Seattle" })
333: };
334: 
335: var modified = original with
336: {
337:     Name = "Johnny Doe",
338:     Addresses = original.Addresses.SetItem("home",
339:         original.Addresses["home"] with { Street = "121 Main St" })
340: };
341: 
342: foreach (var diff in Customer.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(original, modified))
343:     Console.WriteLine(diff);
344: ```
345: 
346: Output:
347: ```
348: Name: John Doe → Johnny Doe
349: Addresses["home"].Street: 123 Main St → 121 Main St
350: ```
351: 
352: ### How it works
353: 
354: `Inequalities()` returns `IEnumerable<Inequality>`, where each `Inequality` has:
355: 
356: - **`Path`** — a `MemberPath` describing which member differs (e.g., `Addresses["home"].Street`)
357: - **`Left`** — the value from the first object
358: - **`Right`** — the value from the second object
359: 
360: Paths are composed of segments:
361: 
362: | Segment | Example | Meaning |
363: |---------|---------|---------|
364: | `Property` | `Name` | A property differs |
365: | `Field` | `_count` | A field differs |
366: | `Index` | `[0]` | An ordered collection element at index |
367: | `Key` | `["home"]` | A dictionary entry by key |
368: | `Added` | `[+]` | An element present only in the right set |
369: | `Removed` | `[-]` | An element present only in the left set |
370: 
371: ### Drill-down
372: 
373: When a collection element or dictionary value is itself an `[Equatable]` type, `Inequalities()` automatically drills down into its properties instead of reporting the entire object as changed. In the example above, the address change is reported as `Addresses["home"].Street` rather than the whole `Address` object.
374: 
375: ### Base path
376: 
377: You can pass a base path to prefix all reported paths — useful when composing inequalities from parent contexts:
378: 
379: ```c#
380: var diffs = Address.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(
381:     addressA, addressB, new MemberPath(new[] { MemberPathSegment.Property("Home") }));
382: // Reports: Home.Street, Home.City, etc.
383: ```
384: 
385: ## Migrating from version 3
386: 
387: ### Inherited Equality Attributes
388: 
389: Version 4 introduces support for inherited equality attributes on overridden properties, making repeating attributes
390: unnecessary. When a child class overrides a virtual property from a parent class, it now automatically inherits the
391: equality attribute (e.g., `[OrderedEquality]`) from the parent. You no longer need to redeclare attributes on overriding
392: properties.
393: 
394: ```c#
395: [Equatable]
396: public partial class Parent
397: {
398:     [OrderedEquality]
399:     public virtual int[] Values { get; set; }
400: }
401: 
402: [Equatable]
403: public partial class Child : Parent
404: {
405:     // Automatically inherits [OrderedEquality] from Parent
406:     public override int[] Values { get; set; }
407: }
408: ```
409: 
410: ### Improved Inheritance Chain Detection
411: 
412: Version 4 improves how `base.Equals()` is called in inheritance hierarchies. Previously, generated code would only
413: call `base.Equals()` if the **immediate** base class had `[Equatable]`. Now, the generator walks the **entire**
414: inheritance chain and calls `base.Equals()` if:
415: 
416: 1. **Any ancestor** has the `[Equatable]` attribute, OR
417: 2. **Any ancestor** has manually overridden `Equals(object)`
418: 
419: This fixes scenarios where equality was incorrectly skipped in multi-level inheritance:
420: 
421: ```c#
422: [Equatable]
423: public partial class GrandParent
424: {
425:     public string Name { get; set; }
426: }
427: 
428: // No [Equatable] - inherits GrandParent's Equals
429: public class Parent : GrandParent
430: {
431:     public int Age { get; set; }
432: }
433: 
434: [Equatable]
435: public partial class Child : Parent
436: {
437:     public string School { get; set; }
438: }
439: ```
440: 
441: **Before (v3):** `Child.Equals()` did NOT call `base.Equals()` because `Parent` lacks `[Equatable]`.
442: Only `School` was compared, ignoring `Name`.
443: 
444: **After (v4):** `Child.Equals()` calls `base.Equals()` because `GrandParent` has `[Equatable]`.
445: Both `School` and `Name` are compared correctly.
446: 
447: ### Ignore Inherited Members
448: 
449: The `IgnoreInheritedMembers` property controls how inherited members are handled:
450: 
451: | IgnoreInheritedMembers | Any Ancestor has [Equatable] | Behavior |
452: |------------------------|------------------------------|----------|
453: | `true`  | N/A | Compare only declared members, type check, no `base.Equals()` |
454: | `false` | Yes | Call `base.Equals()`, let ancestor handle its members |
455: | `false` | No  | Type check + compare ALL inherited properties from entire chain |
456: 
457: ```c#
458: [Equatable(IgnoreInheritedMembers = true)]
459: public partial class Child : Parent
460: {
461:     // Will NOT call base.Equals() even if Parent has [Equatable]
462:     // Only properties defined in Child are compared
463:     public string School { get; set; }
464: }
465: ```
466: 
467: ## Migrating from version 2
468: 
469: Migrating to version 3 is very straightforward.
470: 
471: 1. Ensure projects are targeting C# 9.0 or latter using the MSBuild property `LangVersion`.
472: 2. Be aware that `IEquatable<T>` for classes is now implemented explicitly in order to support deep equality. As a result, the method `Equals(T)` method is no longer marked as public. Most code should still work, requiring only to be recompiled as the ABI has changed.
473: 
474: If you have an existing project using `Generator.Equals` and don't need any of the new features, you can still use version 2.x. The differences are minimal between both major versions.

## Supported Comparers

Below is a list of all supported comparers. Would you like something else added? Let me know by raising an issue or sending a PR!

### Default

This is the comparer that's used when a property has no attributes indicating otherwise. The generated code will use 
```EqualityComparer<T>.Default``` for both equals and hashing operation.

> _Fields are not used in comparison unless explicitly annotated. To enable the default comparison for a field, annotate it with the `DefaultEquality` attribute._

### IgnoreEquality

```c#
[IgnoreEquality] 
public string Name { get; set; }
```

As the name implies, the property is ignored during Equals and GetHashCode calls!


### OrderedEquality

```c#
[OrderedEquality]
public string[] Fruits { get; set; } // Fruits have to be in the same order for the array to be considered equal.
```

This equality comparer will compare properties as a sequence instead of a reference. This works just like ```Enumerable.SequenceEqual```, which assumes both lists are of the same size and same sort.

Bear in mind that the property has to implement IEnumerable<T> and the that the items themselves implement equality (you can use Generator.Equals in the items too!).

You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:

```c#
// Using StringComparison for string collections
[OrderedEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
public string[] Tags { get; set; }

// Using a custom comparer type
[OrderedEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
public string[] Names { get; set; }

// Using a custom IEqualityComparer<T> with a Default static member
[OrderedEquality(typeof(MyCustomComparer))]
public string[] Values { get; set; }
```

### UnorderedEquality

```c#
[UnorderedEquality]
public string[] Fruits { get; set; } // Does not care about the order of the fruits!

[UnorderedEquality]
public IDictionary<string, object> Properties { get; set; } // Works with dictionaries too!
```

This equality comparer will compare properties as an unordered sequence instead of a reference. This works just like ```Enumerable.SequenceEqual```, but it does not care about the order as long as the all values (including the repetitions) are present.

As with OrderedEquality, bear in mind that the property (or key and values if using a dictionary) has to implement IEnumerable<T> and the that the items themselves implement equality (you can use Generator.Equals in the items too!).

You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:

```c#
// Using StringComparison for string collections
[UnorderedEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
public List<string> Tags { get; set; }

// Using a custom comparer type
[UnorderedEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
public List<string> Names { get; set; }
```

### SetEquality

```c#
[SetEquality]
public HashSet<string> Fruits { get; set; } // Fruits can be in any order and duplicates are ignored
```

This equality comparer will do a set comparison, using ```SetEquals``` whenever the underlying collection implements `ISet<T>`, otherwise falling back to manually comparing both collections, which can be expensive for large collections.

You can also specify a custom comparer for the elements:

```c#
// Using StringComparison for string collections
[SetEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
public HashSet<string> Tags { get; set; }

// Using a custom comparer type
[SetEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))]
public HashSet<string> Names { get; set; }
```

Hashing always returns 0 for this type of equality.

### ReferenceEquality

```c#
[ReferenceEquality] 
public string Name { get; set; } // Will only return true if strings are the same reference (eg. when used with string.Intern)
```

This will ignore whatever equality is implemented for a particular object and compare references instead.

### StringEquality

```c#
[StringEquality(StringComparison.CurrentCulture | CurrentCultureIgnoreCase | InvariantCulture | InvariantCultureIgnoreCase | Ordinal | OrdinalIgnoreCase)]
public string Title { get; set; } // Will use the StringComparison set in constructor when comparing strings
```

### PrecisionEquality

```c#
[PrecisionEquality(0.001)]
public double Temperature { get; set; } // Equal if Math.Abs(a - b) < 0.001

[PrecisionEquality(5)]
public int Score { get; set; } // Equal if Math.Abs(a - b) < 5

[PrecisionEquality(0.001)]
public double? NullableValue { get; set; } // Handles nulls: both null = equal, one null = not equal
```

This equality comparer uses a tolerance (epsilon) to compare numeric values. Two values are considered equal when their absolute difference is less than the specified precision. This is excluded from `GetHashCode` since there is no stable bucketing under tolerance.

Supported types: `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `int`, `long`, `short`, `sbyte`, and their nullable variants.

### CustomEquality

```c#
class LengthEqualityComparer : IEqualityComparer<string>
{
    public static readonly LengthEqualityComparer Default = new();

    public bool Equals(string? x, string? y) => x?.Length == y?.Length;

    public int GetHashCode(string obj) => obj.Length.GetHashCode();
}

class NameEqualityComparer 
{
    public static readonly IEqualityComparer<string> Default = new SomeCustomComparer();
}


[CustomEquality(typeof(LengthEqualityComparer))] 
public string Name1 { get; set; } // Will use LengthEqualityComparer to compare the values of Name1.

[CustomEquality(typeof(NameEqualityComparer))] 
public string Name2 { get; set; } // Will use NameEqualityComparer.Default to compare values of Name2.

[CustomEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase))] 
public string Name2 { get; set; } // Will use StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase to compare values of Name2.
```

This attribute allows you to specify a custom comparer for a particular property. For it to work, the type passed as an
argument to CustomEqualityAttribute should fulfill AT LEAST one of the following:

* Have a static field/property named Default returning a valid IEqualityComparer<T> instance for the target type;
* Have a static field/property with the same name passed to the CustomComparerAttribute returning a valid IEqualityComparer<T> instance for the target type;
* Implement IEqualityComparer<T> and expose a parameterless constructor.

## Advanced Options

### Explicit Mode

The generator allows you to explicitly specify which properties are used to generate the `IEquatable`.  

To do this, set the `Explicit` property of `EquatableAttribute` to `true` and specify the required properties using `DefaultEqualityAttribute` or other attributes.
```cs
using Generator.Equals;

[Equatable(Explicit = true)]
partial class MyClass
{
    // Only this property will be used for equality!
    [DefaultEquality] 
    public string Name { get; set; } = "Konstantin"; 
    
    public string Description { get; set; } = "";
}
```


### Ignore Inherited Members

By default (`IgnoreInheritedMembers = false`), the generated code handles inherited members as follows:
- If any ancestor has `[Equatable]` or a custom `Equals` override, `base.Equals()` is called to delegate equality
- If NO ancestor has `[Equatable]`, all inherited properties from the entire chain are explicitly compared

Set `IgnoreInheritedMembers = true` to skip calling `base.Equals()` and ignore all inherited properties.
This is useful when you want to completely redefine equality for a derived class without considering
the base class's properties.

```cs
using Generator.Equals;

[Equatable]
partial class Person
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

[Equatable(IgnoreInheritedMembers = true)]
partial class Doctor : Person
{
    // Will NOT call base.Equals(), so Person.Name is not compared.
    // Only Id and Specialization are used for equality.
    public string Id { get; set; }
    public string Specialization { get; set; }
}
```

## Inequalities

Every `[Equatable]` type gets a generated `EqualityComparer` with an `Inequalities()` method that returns exactly which members differ between two instances — with full member paths, including nested objects, collection indices, and dictionary keys.

```c#
[Equatable]
partial record Customer
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }
    [UnorderedEquality] public required ImmutableDictionary<string, Address> Addresses { get; init; }
}

[Equatable]
partial record Address
{
    public required string Street { get; init; }
    public required string City { get; init; }
}
```

```c#
var original = new Customer
{
    Name = "John Doe",
    Addresses = ImmutableDictionary<string, Address>.Empty
        .Add("home", new Address { Street = "123 Main St", City = "Seattle" })
};

var modified = original with
{
    Name = "Johnny Doe",
    Addresses = original.Addresses.SetItem("home",
        original.Addresses["home"] with { Street = "121 Main St" })
};

foreach (var diff in Customer.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(original, modified))
    Console.WriteLine(diff);
```

Output:
```
Name: John Doe → Johnny Doe
Addresses["home"].Street: 123 Main St → 121 Main St
```

### How it works

`Inequalities()` returns `IEnumerable<Inequality>`, where each `Inequality` has:

- **`Path`** — a `MemberPath` describing which member differs (e.g., `Addresses["home"].Street`)
- **`Left`** — the value from the first object
- **`Right`** — the value from the second object

Paths are composed of segments:

| Segment | Example | Meaning |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `Property` | `Name` | A property differs |
| `Field` | `_count` | A field differs |
| `Index` | `[0]` | An ordered collection element at index |
| `Key` | `["home"]` | A dictionary entry by key |
| `Added` | `[+]` | An element present only in the right set |
| `Removed` | `[-]` | An element present only in the left set |

### Drill-down

When a collection element or dictionary value is itself an `[Equatable]` type, `Inequalities()` automatically drills down into its properties instead of reporting the entire object as changed. In the example above, the address change is reported as `Addresses["home"].Street` rather than the whole `Address` object.

### Base path

You can pass a base path to prefix all reported paths — useful when composing inequalities from parent contexts:

```c#
var diffs = Address.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(
    addressA, addressB, new MemberPath(new[] { MemberPathSegment.Property("Home") }));
// Reports: Home.Street, Home.City, etc.
```

## Migrating from version 3

### Inherited Equality Attributes

Version 4 introduces support for inherited equality attributes on overridden properties, making repeating attributes
unnecessary. When a child class overrides a virtual property from a parent class, it now automatically inherits the
equality attribute (e.g., `[OrderedEquality]`) from the parent. You no longer need to redeclare attributes on overriding
properties.

```c#
[Equatable]
public partial class Parent
{
    [OrderedEquality]
    public virtual int[] Values { get; set; }
}

[Equatable]
public partial class Child : Parent
{
    // Automatically inherits [OrderedEquality] from Parent
    public override int[] Values { get; set; }
}
```

### Improved Inheritance Chain Detection

Version 4 improves how `base.Equals()` is called in inheritance hierarchies. Previously, generated code would only
call `base.Equals()` if the **immediate** base class had `[Equatable]`. Now, the generator walks the **entire**
inheritance chain and calls `base.Equals()` if:

1. **Any ancestor** has the `[Equatable]` attribute, OR
2. **Any ancestor** has manually overridden `Equals(object)`

This fixes scenarios where equality was incorrectly skipped in multi-level inheritance:

```c#
[Equatable]
public partial class GrandParent
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

// No [Equatable] - inherits GrandParent's Equals
public class Parent : GrandParent
{
    public int Age { get; set; }
}

[Equatable]
public partial class Child : Parent
{
    public string School { get; set; }
}
```

**Before (v3):** `Child.Equals()` did NOT call `base.Equals()` because `Parent` lacks `[Equatable]`.
Only `School` was compared, ignoring `Name`.

**After (v4):** `Child.Equals()` calls `base.Equals()` because `GrandParent` has `[Equatable]`.
Both `School` and `Name` are compared correctly.

### Ignore Inherited Members

The `IgnoreInheritedMembers` property controls how inherited members are handled:

| IgnoreInheritedMembers | Any Ancestor has [Equatable] | Behavior |
|------------------------|------------------------------|----------|
| `true`  | N/A | Compare only declared members, type check, no `base.Equals()` |
| `false` | Yes | Call `base.Equals()`, let ancestor handle its members |
| `false` | No  | Type check + compare ALL inherited properties from entire chain |

```c#
[Equatable(IgnoreInheritedMembers = true)]
public partial class Child : Parent
{
    // Will NOT call base.Equals() even if Parent has [Equatable]
    // Only properties defined in Child are compared
    public string School { get; set; }
}
```

7: # Generator.Equals
8: 
9: C# source generator that auto-implements `IEquatable<T>`, `Equals()`, `GetHashCode()`, `==`/`!=` operators, and an `Inequalities()` diff method at compile time using attributes. No runtime reflection.
10: 
11: ## Setup
12: 
13: Add both packages:
14: 
15: ```xml
16: <PackageReference Include="Generator.Equals" PrivateAssets="all" />
17: <PackageReference Include="Generator.Equals.Runtime" />
18: ```
19: 
20: Requires C# 9.0+. The type **must be `partial`**.
21: 
22: ## Attributes Quick Reference
23: 
24: ### Type-level
25: 
26: | Attribute | Purpose |
27: |-----------|---------|
28: | `[Equatable]` | Generates equality members for the type |
29: | `[Equatable(Explicit = true)]` | Only compare properties with explicit equality attributes |
30: | `[Equatable(IgnoreInheritedMembers = true)]` | Skip base class members entirely |
31: 
32: ### Property/Field-level
33: 
34: | Attribute | Use When |
35: |-----------|----------|
36: | `[DefaultEquality]` | Default comparer. **Required on fields** (fields are excluded by default). |
37: | `[IgnoreEquality]` | Skip this member |
38: | `[OrderedEquality]` | Compare collection elements in order (like `SequenceEqual`) |
39: | `[UnorderedEquality]` | Compare collection elements ignoring order |
40: | `[SetEquality]` | Compare as sets (duplicates ignored) |
41: | `[ReferenceEquality]` | Compare by reference only |
42: | `[StringEquality(StringComparison.X)]` | String-specific comparison (string props only) |
43: | `[PrecisionEquality(0.001)]` | Tolerance-based numeric comparison |
44: | `[CustomEquality(typeof(MyComparer))]` | Custom `IEqualityComparer<T>` |
45: 
46: ### Comparer constructor patterns (for collection and custom attributes)
47: 
48: ```csharp
49: [OrderedEquality]                                                          // Default comparer
50: [OrderedEquality(typeof(MyComparer))]                                     // Type with static Default member
51: [OrderedEquality(typeof(StringComparer), nameof(StringComparer.Ordinal))] // Named static member
52: [OrderedEquality(StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)]                     // StringComparison shorthand
53: ```
54: 
55: ## Best Practices
56: 
57: ### Always annotate collection properties
58: 
59: ```csharp
60: // WRONG - produces diagnostic GE001
61: public List<int> Items { get; set; }
62: 
63: // RIGHT
64: [OrderedEquality]
65: public List<int> Items { get; set; }
66: ```
67: 
68: ### Use Explicit mode when only a few properties matter
69: 
70: ```csharp
71: [Equatable(Explicit = true)]
72: partial class User
73: {
74:     [DefaultEquality] public string Id { get; set; }     // Compared
75:     public string DisplayName { get; set; }               // Ignored
76:     public DateTime LastLogin { get; set; }               // Ignored
77: }
78: ```
79: 
80: ### Mark fields explicitly
81: 
82: Fields are **not** included by default. You must annotate them:
83: 
84: ```csharp
85: [DefaultEquality]
86: private int _version;
87: ```
88: 
89: ### Use the generated EqualityComparer
90: 
91: Every `[Equatable]` type gets a nested `EqualityComparer` class:
92: 
93: ```csharp
94: // Use in dictionaries, HashSets, LINQ
95: var dict = new Dictionary<MyType, string>(MyType.EqualityComparer.Default);
96: var distinct = items.Distinct(MyType.EqualityComparer.Default);
97: ```
98: 
99: ### Use Inequalities for diff/audit
100: 
101: ```csharp
102: foreach (var diff in MyType.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(oldObj, newObj))
103:     Console.WriteLine(diff);
104: // Output: Name: John -> Jane
105: // Output: Addresses["home"].Street: 123 Main St -> 456 Oak Ave
106: ```
107: 
108: Nested `[Equatable]` objects in collections are auto-drilled — you get per-field diffs, not "entire object changed".
109: 
110: ## Common Pitfalls
111: 
112: 1. **Non-partial type** (GE006) — The type MUST be declared `partial`.
113: 
114: 2. **Manual Equals/GetHashCode** (GE005) — Do NOT override `Equals()` or `GetHashCode()` manually on an `[Equatable]` type. The generator owns these.
115: 
116: 3. **Conflicting collection attributes** (GE007) — Only ONE of `[OrderedEquality]`, `[UnorderedEquality]`, `[SetEquality]` per property.
117: 
118: 4. **Hash code instability** — `[UnorderedEquality]`, `[SetEquality]`, and `[PrecisionEquality]` return hash code 0 or exclude from hashing. Types using these are poor dictionary keys.
119: 
120: 5. **Inheritance with [Equatable]** — The generator walks the full inheritance chain. If any ancestor has `[Equatable]` or overrides `Equals()`, it calls `base.Equals()`. Use `IgnoreInheritedMembers = true` to opt out.
121: 
122: 6. **Overriding properties inherits attributes** — A `Child` overriding a `Parent`'s `[OrderedEquality] virtual int[] Values` automatically inherits `[OrderedEquality]`. Do NOT re-annotate unless you want to change behavior.
123: 
124: 7. **`[StringEquality]` on non-string** (GE008) — Only valid on `string` properties.
125: 
126: 8. **`[PrecisionEquality]` types** (GE010) — Only `float`, `double`, `decimal`, `int`, `long`, `short`, `sbyte` and their nullable variants.
127: 
128: ## Examples
129: 
130: ### Basic class
131: 
132: ```csharp
133: [Equatable]
134: partial class Person
135: {
136:     public string Name { get; set; }
137:     public int Age { get; set; }
138: 
139:     [IgnoreEquality]
140:     public DateTime LastUpdated { get; set; }
141: }
142: ```
143: 
144: ### Record with collections
145: 
146: ```csharp
147: [Equatable]
148: partial record Customer(
149:     string Id,
150:     string Name,
151:     [property: OrderedEquality] ImmutableArray<Address> Addresses,

156: ### Struct with custom comparer
157:

159: [Equatable]
160: partial struct Coordinate
161: {

163:     public double Latitude { get; set; }
164: 
165:     [PrecisionEquality(0.0001)]
166:     public double Longitude { get; set; }
167: }
168: ```
169: 
170: ### Inheritance
171: 
172: ```csharp
173: [Equatable]
174: partial class Animal
175: {
176:     public string Species { get; set; }
177: }
178: 
179: [Equatable]
180: partial class Pet : Animal
181: {
182:     public string Name { get; set; }
183:     // Species is also compared via base.Equals()
184: }
185: ```
186: 
187: ### Diff / Inequalities
188: 
189: ```csharp
190: var diffs = Customer.EqualityComparer.Default.Inequalities(before, after);
191: foreach (var d in diffs)
192: {
193:     // d.Path  — e.g., "Addresses[0].Street"
194:     // d.Left  — old value
195:     // d.Right — new value
196:     Console.WriteLine(d);

198: ```

211: | GE009 | Collection attribute on non-collection |
